questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of the design mix?
options: The three elements a business balances when designing a product: function, aesthetics and cost
The combination of product, price, promotion and place
The range of products a business sells
The materials used to manufacture a product
questions.why: Function, aesthetics and economic manufacture are the three pulls on any design, and they trade off against each other.
whyNot: That is the marketing mix, the four Ps. The design mix has three elements and is about the product itself.
That is the product portfolio.
Materials are one input into the cost element, not the whole design mix.

questions.stem: Which term is defined as: how a product appeals to the senses, including its appearance and feel?
options: Aesthetics
Function
Economic manufacture
Ethical sourcing
questions.why: Aesthetics covers look, feel, weight, finish, smell and even sound. It is how businesses differentiate when function is similar across a market.
whyNot: Function is how well the product does the job it was designed for.
Economic manufacture is whether it can be made cheaply enough to sell profitably.
Ethical sourcing is about how the materials were obtained, not how the product appeals.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of economic manufacture?
options: Designing a product so it can be made at a cost low enough to sell profitably
Making a product in the cheapest country available
Designing a product that uses recycled materials only
Selling a product at the lowest price in the market
questions.why: Economic manufacture is the cost element of the design mix. A design that cannot be made at a viable cost has failed on a design criterion, not just a financial one.
whyNot: Where it is made is a location decision. Economic manufacture is about designing for a viable cost wherever it is produced.
Recycled content relates to resource depletion, which is a separate pressure on design.
That is a pricing strategy, not a design decision.

questions.stem: Which term is defined as: designing and producing in a way that creates as little waste as possible?
options: Waste minimisation
Recycling
Re-use
Resource depletion
questions.why: Minimisation means using less material in the first place, such as lighter packaging or fewer components. It usually cuts cost as well as waste.
whyNot: Recycling recovers materials after use. Minimisation avoids using them at all.
Re-use means using the same item again, such as a refillable container.
Resource depletion is the problem these three approaches respond to.

questions.stem: A business redesigns a product using cheaper materials. What is the most likely trade-off?
options: Lower cost but weaker function or aesthetics
Lower cost with no effect on the other elements
Higher cost and better function
Better aesthetics and better function
questions.why: The design mix trades off. Cutting the cost element almost always takes something from function or appearance, and identifying which is what earns the analysis mark.
whyNot: Nothing in the design mix changes in isolation. That is the whole point of calling it a mix.
Cheaper materials lower cost. They do not raise it.
Cheaper materials rarely improve either function or appearance.

questions.stem: For an industrial machine sold to other businesses, which element of the design mix is most likely to lead?
options: Function
Aesthetics
Ethical sourcing
Viral appeal
questions.why: Business buyers judge on reliability, performance and total cost of ownership. Appearance matters far less than whether the machine works and keeps working.
whyNot: Aesthetics leads in luxury and consumer markets, not usually in industrial ones.
Ethical sourcing is an increasing pressure but rarely the leading design criterion for industrial equipment.
Viral appeal is a promotional idea, not an element of the design mix.

questions.stem: Why can designing for waste minimisation reduce costs as well as waste?
options: Using less material means buying less material
Waste disposal is always free
Recycled materials are always cheaper than new ones
Customers will pay more for any product with less packaging
questions.why: Less material is a direct saving on inputs, and often on transport too because the product is lighter. This is a useful evaluation point because it undercuts the assumption that sustainable design always costs more.
whyNot: Disposal normally costs money, which is another reason minimisation saves.
Sometimes true, sometimes not. Recycled inputs can cost more where collection and processing are expensive.
Some customers will pay more, many will not. Never assume willingness to pay without evidence.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of ethical sourcing?
options: Buying materials in a way that respects the pay, conditions and environment of suppliers
Buying materials from the cheapest available supplier
Buying only materials that can be recycled
Buying materials produced in the same country as the business
questions.why: Ethical sourcing is about the conditions under which inputs are produced: fair pay, safe conditions, no child labour, no illegal environmental damage.
whyNot: That is cost minimisation, which is often what ethical sourcing has to be weighed against.
Recyclability relates to resource depletion, a separate consideration.
That is local sourcing, which may or may not be ethical.

questions.stem: What is the main practical difficulty a business faces in guaranteeing ethical sourcing?
options: Supply chains are long and opaque, so verification is difficult and expensive
Ethical sourcing is illegal in most countries
It always makes the product worse
Customers never care about it
questions.why: A business may know its direct supplier but not that supplier's suppliers. Auditing several tiers back costs real money, and that is why scandals still happen to firms that believed they were compliant.
whyNot: The opposite: much of it is increasingly required by law.
It affects cost and sometimes availability, but not the product's function or appearance.
Consumer and retailer pressure is precisely why businesses invest in it.

questions.stem: A luxury watch brand is deciding whether to cut manufacturing costs by 20%. Which consideration is most important?
options: Whether the cost saving damages the aesthetics and perceived quality the price depends on
Whether the watch will still tell the time accurately
Whether the packaging can be recycled
Whether the factory is in a trading bloc
questions.why: For a premium product, aesthetics and perceived quality are what justify the price. A 20% cost saving that customers can see or feel could destroy far more value in price than it saves in cost.
whyNot: Function matters, but at this price point it is the minimum expectation rather than the differentiator.
Relevant to sustainability but secondary to whether the brand position survives.
A location and tariff question, not the central design trade-off here.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of designing for re-use rather than recycling?
options: A refillable glass bottle returned to the producer
A plastic bottle made from a single material so it can be reprocessed
Packaging made thinner to use less plastic
A product made from recycled aluminium
questions.why: Re-use means the same item is used again in its existing form. The refillable bottle goes back and is refilled rather than being broken down.
whyNot: Single-material design is to make recycling possible, which means reprocessing rather than re-using.
That is waste minimisation: using less material in the first place.
That is using recycled input, which is the output end of recycling.

questions.stem: Why does good design link directly to added value?
options: Design can raise the price customers will pay without raising bought-in material costs by as much
Design always reduces the cost of materials to zero
Added value is calculated from the design budget
Design has no effect on price
questions.why: Added value is selling price minus bought-in materials and services. Better design can lift the price customers accept by more than it lifts input cost, so the gap widens.
whyNot: Design cannot eliminate material costs, only reduce or change them.
Added value is price minus bought-in costs. The design budget does not appear in the formula at all.
Design is one of the main reasons customers accept a higher price.

questions.stem: A product is sold into a hot, humid, salt-air island environment. Which design consideration becomes most important?
options: Function, specifically resistance to corrosion
Aesthetics, specifically colour choice
Viral marketing potential
The number of components
questions.why: If the product corrodes and fails in two years rather than ten, nothing else about the design matters. The environment makes durability the deciding criterion, which is why specification beats appearance in that market.
whyNot: Colour may matter to appeal but not to whether the product survives the conditions.
A promotional consideration, not a design one.
Component count affects cost and reliability indirectly, but corrosion resistance is the direct issue here.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of resource depletion?
options: Using up finite natural resources faster than they can be replaced
The cost of raw materials rising over time
A business running out of cash
Reducing the number of products in a portfolio
questions.why: Depletion is about the physical exhaustion of finite resources, which is what drives the design pressure towards minimisation, re-use and recycling.
whyNot: Rising input prices may be a consequence of depletion, but they are not the definition.
That is a liquidity problem, unrelated to natural resources.
That is portfolio rationalisation.
